# Abstract

Government healthcare expenditure is often associated with better population health outcomes, but the strength of this relationship may differ across countries and may reflect broader economic and regional differences. This study examines whether government healthcare expenditure is associated with life expectancy across countries from 2007 to 2017, and whether this relationship remains after accounting for GDP per capita, region, and year. Using 601 country-year observations from 64 countries, we estimate a simple linear regression model to examine the unadjusted relationship and a multiple linear regression model to examine the relationship after including the control variables. The simple model shows a positive and statistically significant association between government healthcare expenditure and life expectancy, supporting H1. However, the association becomes much smaller and is no longer statistically significant in the multiple regression model, so H2 is not supported. Overall, the findings suggest that healthcare expenditure alone does not fully explain cross-country differences in life expectancy and should be understood within a broader economic and national context.

# Introduction

Health is a fundamental part of human well-being and an important concern for individuals, governments, and public policy. The World Health Organization defines health as “a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity” (Public Health Agency of Canada, 2017). However, population health outcomes are shaped by a wide range of factors, including income, education, social and physical environments, and access to health services (Public Health Agency of Canada, 2017). Understanding how public healthcare investment relates to population health is therefore important for evaluating health systems and informing public policy.

Government healthcare expenditure represents one way in which countries invest public resources in population health. Greater public spending may improve access to healthcare services, disease prevention, treatment quality, and overall health system capacity, which may contribute to longer life expectancy. At the same time, countries differ substantially in their level of economic development, geographic context, and changes in health outcomes over time. These broader differences may influence both healthcare expenditure and life expectancy.

This project therefore examines the relationship between government healthcare expenditure and life expectancy across countries between 2007 and 2017. Life expectancy is used as a broad measure of population health because it reflects how long people are expected to live under current mortality conditions. Government healthcare expenditure is measured as a percentage of GDP, representing the share of national economic resources allocated by governments to healthcare.

# Relevant Literature

Previous research generally suggests a positive association between healthcare expenditure and population health, although the strength of this relationship varies across settings. Studies of developing European Union countries have found a long-run relationship between public health expenditure and health outcomes. Greater public health expenditure is associated with higher life expectancy and lower infant mortality @onofrei2021. Similar evidence has been reported among OECD countries, where government health expenditure has been positively associated with life expectancy @anwar2023. Together, these findings suggest that greater investment in healthcare may contribute to better population health outcomes, supporting the expectation of a positive relationship between government healthcare expenditure and life expectancy.

However, the literature also shows that higher healthcare spending does not produce the same outcomes across countries. Research in the Middle East and North Africa has found that some countries spend relatively more on healthcare without achieving correspondingly higher life expectancy, suggesting that the allocation and efficiency of healthcare resources may also matter @balkhi2021. Meanwhile, a study of 175 countries also found that the relationship between health spending and life expectancy varies across countries. The benefits of additional health spending differ depending on a country’s level of life expectancy @obrizan2018. These findings indicate that expenditure alone may not fully explain international differences in population health.

One important explanation for these differences is that life expectancy is influenced by broader economic and country-level conditions. Longitudinal research across OECD countries identifies not only healthcare expenditure, but also GDP, healthcare resources, social spending, demographic factors, and other contextual characteristics as important correlates of life expectancy @roffia2023. Anwar et al. also find that income, measured through GDP per capita, is positively associated with life expectancy alongside healthcare expenditure @anwar2023. This suggests that an observed relationship between healthcare expenditure and life expectancy may partly reflect differences in national economic development rather than healthcare expenditure alone.

Therefore, to conclude, healthcare expenditure is generally associated with higher life expectancy, but this relationship is not uniform across countries and regions. Besides, economic and country differences mean that similar levels of healthcare spending are associated with different health outcomes. Much of the existing research focuses on particular groups of countries, such as developing EU countries, the MENA region, or OECD members, although some studies have examined broader international samples.

Building on this literature, our study examines government healthcare expenditure and life expectancy across 64 countries from 2007 to 2017. In addition to estimating the unadjusted relationship between the two variables, we extend the analysis by controlling for GDP per capita,region,and year. This allows us to examine whether the positive association between government healthcare expenditure and life expectancy remains after accounting for differences in economic development, geographic context, and changes over time.

# Research Question and Hypotheses

This research aims to address two research questions by stating two related hypotheses.

RQ1: How is government health expenditure associated with life expectancy across countries from 2007 to 2017?

Based on the expectation that greater public healthcare spending may improve access to healthcare services, disease prevention, treatment quality, and overall health system capacity, we propose the following hypothesis:

H1: Countries with higher government healthcare expenditure as a percentage of GDP tend to have higher life expectancy.

This first research question examines the overall, unadjusted association between government healthcare expenditure and life expectancy.

RQ2: Does the relationship between government healthcare expenditure and life expectancy remain after accounting for GDP per capita, regional differences, and changes over time?

Because national income, geographic differences, and general changes over time may also be associated with population health, the final analysis incorporates GDP per capita, region, and year as control variables. We therefore propose a second hypothesis:

H2: The positive association between government healthcare expenditure and life expectancy will remain after accounting for GDP per capita, region, and year.

Together, the two research questions allow us to compare the overall relationship between government healthcare expenditure and life expectancy with the relationship that remains after accounting for major country-level differences. Because the data are observational, the analysis focuses on associations rather than claiming a direct causal effect of government healthcare expenditure on life expectancy.

# Dataset and Methods

## Dataset

This study combines three international datasets to examine the relationship between government healthcare expenditure and life expectancy across countries between 2007 and 2017.

The main explanatory variable was obtained from the World Bank Data360 platform using the International Monetary Fund (IMF) Government Finance Statistics indicator \*\*IMF_COFOG_GEL_GF07 (Government Expenditure on Health)\*\*, which measures general government healthcare expenditure as a percentage of GDP @worldbank_health. The main outcome variable was obtained from the World Bank Data360 indicator \*\*WEF_GCIHH_LIFEEXPECT\*\*, which reports life expectancy measured in years @worldbank_life. To account for differences in national economic development, GDP per capita was obtained from the World Bank World Development Indicators (WDI) using indicator \*\*WB_WDI_NY_GDP_PCAP_CD\*\* @worldbank_gdp. A regional classification variable was additionally generated from ISO3 country codes using the \`countrycode\` R package.

The unit of analysis is the country-year. After cleaning and standardizing the three datasets, they were merged using ISO3 country codes and year to construct the final analytical dataset. The final dataset contains 601 country-year observations across 64 countries covering the period from 2007 to 2017.

One limitation of the dataset is that the historical Government Health Expenditure indicator (2007–2017) is no longer publicly available through the current World Bank Data360 or IMF Government Finance Statistics interfaces. In addition, because the final analysis requires complete information across all model variables, only countries with complete observations were retained in the analytical sample.

## Data Preparation

Data acquisition, cleaning, and merging were performed using reproducible R scripts within an R Project workflow. Life expectancy and GDP per capita data were downloaded directly from the World Bank Data360 platform using documented API requests and stored locally before analysis. The historical Government Health Expenditure dataset (IMF_COFOG_GEL_GF07) was originally downloaded during the project proposal stage. During preparation of the final project, attempts were made to reproduce the original download through both the current World Bank Data360 platform and the IMF Government Finance Statistics (GFS) Data Explorer. Because the historical 2007–2017 observations are no longer publicly accessible, the archived CSV retained from the proposal stage was used with instructor approval. The original data source, indicator information, retrieval process, and verification steps are documented in the project repository.

Each dataset was cleaned separately prior to merging. All datasets were restricted to the common study period of 2007–2017. For the health expenditure dataset, only general government expenditure observations measured as a percentage of GDP were retained. For the life expectancy dataset, observations reported in years were retained. GDP per capita observations were restricted to valid positive values, and the natural logarithm of GDP per capita was calculated because the original variable exhibited substantial right skewness. Country identifiers were standardized using ISO3 country codes, duplicate country-year observations were removed, and a regional classification variable was derived from ISO3 country codes using the \`countrycode\` package.

The cleaned datasets were merged using country code and year. A complete-case analytical dataset was then created by retaining only observations with complete information for all variables included in the regression analysis. The resulting dataset contained 601 country-year observations across 64 countries and was used for all subsequent exploratory analyses and regression models.

## Methods

### Software

All data acquisition, cleaning, merging, exploratory analysis, and statistical modelling were conducted in R @Rsoftware2024. Data manipulation and visualization were performed using the tidyverse collection of packages @tidyverse2019, including readr @readr2024, dplyr @dplyr2026, and tibble @tibble2023. Reproducible file paths were managed using here @here2025. Initial data inspection and cleaning used janitor @janitor2024. API-based data retrieval was implemented using httr2 @httr22025, regional classifications were generated using countrycode @countrycode2018, and regression model outputs were summarized using broom @broom2026.

# Results and Findings

# Discussion and Conclusion

The findings suggest that government healthcare expenditure should not be considered alone when comparing life expectancy across countries. Although countries that spend more on public healthcare tend to have higher life expectancy in the unadjusted analysis, this relationship becomes much weaker after accounting for broader country-level differences. This does not mean that healthcare spending is unimportant. Instead, it suggests that population health depends on a wider economic and social context, and that similar levels of healthcare spending may be associated with different outcomes across countries.

The research limitations come from the scope of the research question itself. First, life expectancy is a broad measure of population health. It summarizes mortality conditions but does not capture other important outcomes such as quality of life, disability, access to care, or differences in health across groups within the same country. Second, healthcare spending may affect health outcomes over many years. Spending in one year may therefore not be immediately reflected in life expectancy in that same year. In addition, countries organize and use healthcare resources differently. Two countries with similar spending levels may invest in different services, populations, or types of care, which may lead to different health outcomes.

The study also focuses on country-level averages. These national measures can hide important differences within countries, such as differences by income, age, gender, or location. In addition, the study covers only 2007 to 2017, so the findings describe a specific period and may not fully reflect more recent healthcare systems, technologies, or public health challenges.

Future research could examine more detailed health outcomes in addition to life expectancy, consider possible time lags between healthcare investment and health outcomes, and study how healthcare spending is allocated across different services. More recent data and subgroup-level data could also help explain why the same level of healthcare investment may produce different outcomes across countries and populations.

Overall, our results suggest that the important question is not simply whether countries spend more on healthcare, but also how, where, and under what conditions those resources are used. Healthcare expenditure is one component of population health, but it should be understood in the broader context in which healthcare systems operate.
